claim: If the JWKS holds one entry that makes PyJWK raise something other than PyJWTError (for example a non-string `alg` such as `["RS256"]`), or a body whose JSON nests deeper than the recursion limit, the exception gets past both the per-key skip and `_refresh`'s handler. No `jwks` line names the cause, the usable keys in the same set are thrown away, and the request that triggered the fetch gets a bare 500 instead of 503 with Retry-After.
evidence: auth.py `_fetch`: `try: parsed = PyJWK(jwk) except jwt.PyJWTError: continue  # a key PyJWT can't use for signatures`. But PyJWK looks the algorithm up with `get_default_algorithms()[algorithm]` and catches only KeyError, so a list-valued `alg` raises TypeError (checked: `PyJWK({'kty':'RSA','kid':'x','alg':['RS256'],'n':'AQAB','e':'AQAB'})` -> TypeError). Likewise `json.loads('['*200000)` -> RecursionError, a RuntimeError, while the body stays under MAX_JWKS_BYTES. `_refresh` catches only `(httpx2.HTTPError, ValueError, _JwksError)`, so `log.event("jwks", ..., outcome="failed", reason=...)` is never written, after `_last_attempt` has already been set. The exception then leaves `Verifier.verify_token`, which catches only `_Refused`, and reaches app.py `Wrapper._mcp`'s `except Exception` (logged as a generic `error`, then the held Starlette 500 is sent). Reproduced in the scratchpad: a JWKS of one good RSA key plus a copy with `alg: ["RS256"]`, served by an httpx2 MockTransport. `JwksCache.key("good")` raised TypeError and no `jwks` line was written. In a deployment with this set, one request every 30 s gets 500 'internal error'. Every other request gets 503 (cache never fresh, refetch rate-limited), or 401 'unknown key' after a rotation, and never a `jwks` line saying why. The good key in the same response is never used. REQ-002-PRS-NF008 asks for a `jwks` line for each fetch with the reason of a failed one.
proposal: Test (tests/unit, JwksCache with an httpx2.MockTransport): a JWKS of one valid RSA key and one entry with `alg: ["RS256"]` gives `key("good")` that key and writes `jwks` outcome fetched, keys=1. A body of `'[' * 200000` writes one `jwks` line with outcome failed and raises KeysUnavailable (503 through the app), not RecursionError. Change: in `_fetch`, skip a key on any `Exception` from `PyJWK(jwk)`, not only `jwt.PyJWTError`, or check that `alg` is a str or absent before calling it. In `_refresh`, add `RecursionError` to the caught types, or parse inside `_fetch` and turn a RecursionError into `_JwksError("too deep")`, so every failed fetch writes its `jwks` line and ends in KeysUnavailable.

verdict.reproduction: Per-key skip, src/enterich/auth.py:134-137: `try: parsed = PyJWK(jwk) ... except jwt.PyJWTError: continue  # a key PyJWT can't use for signatures`. Fetch handler, src/enterich/auth.py:100-106: `self._last_attempt = self._clock()` then `except (httpx2.HTTPError, ValueError, _JwksError) as exc: ... log.event("jwks", logging.WARNING, outcome="failed", reason=reason, keys=0)`. The parse at auth.py:121 `data: object = json.loads(body)` comes after the size cap only, so no depth check. Verifier.verify_token (auth.py:155-159) catches only `_Refused`. app.py:160 catches `KeysUnavailable` (503), and anything else goes to app.py:169-172 `except Exception` -> `_respond(send, 500, {"error": "internal error"})`. The tests already state the intent: tests/unit/test_auth.py:285 `test_an_unusable_key_doesnt_hide_the_keys_after_it` and :388 `test_a_failed_jwks_fetch_logs_why`. What I ran: a throwaway pytest file in the scratchpad (/tmp/claude-1000/-home-ubuntu-dev-enterich/0431a6bc-d8e6-4381-9c7d-b9072faa4363/scratchpad/v/test_scratch.py), using tests/conftest.py fixtures and tests/fakes/jwks.FakeJwks. (1) FakeJwks with extra_keys=[copy of signer.jwk() with kid "bad" and alg ["RS256"], signer.jwk()]: Verifier.verify_token(token(signer)) raised `TypeError cannot use 'list' as a dict key`, and logs.events("jwks") == []. The good key was never used. (2) MockTransport returning 200 with body b"[" * 200000 (under MAX_JWKS_BYTES): verify_token raised RecursionError (not KeysUnavailable), and logs.events("jwks") == [].
verdict.reason: I ran both inputs and the finding holds. In src/enterich/auth.py:136, `_fetch` skips a key only on jwt.PyJWTError. A non-string `alg` makes PyJWK raise TypeError, which gets past that skip. In `_refresh` (auth.py:103), only HTTPError, ValueError and _JwksError are caught, and a too-deep JSON body raises RecursionError, which gets past it too. In both cases no `jwks` line is written, although REQ-002-PRS-NF008 asks for one per fetch with the reason of a failed one. The usable key in the same set is thrown away, which goes against the intent that test_auth.py:285 states. `_last_attempt` has already been set by then, so the request ends in app.py:169's generic 500 instead of a 503 with Retry-After. Nothing earlier rules these inputs out. The JWKS is the configured authorization server's, so in practice this is unlikely, but it is a real robustness and logging gap. Nothing in the backlog or an ADR covers it. A unit test in tests/unit/test_auth.py, next to the existing JWKS tests, fails on the current code, and widening the per-key catch plus turning RecursionError into a failed fetch closes it without touching any spec.

claim: When a write request (the PUT of an update, or the comment's POST) has already reached ERPNext, a later read timeout or broken connection is reported with the same text a read gets, "can't be reached" or "didn't answer". That text implies nothing was written, so the agent is told an update failed, or that the draft's comment "couldn't be added", when ERPNext may have saved it.
evidence: src/enterich/erpnext.py:_call has `except TimeoutError: raise ErpnextError(f"ERPNext didn't answer within {CALL_TIMEOUT:g} seconds.")` and `except httpx2.HTTPError as exc: raise ErpnextError(f"ERPNext can't be reached ({type(exc).__name__}).")`. Both apply to every method, whether `method` is GET, POST or PUT, and they fire after `self._client.stream(method, path, ..., content=content)` has sent the body, for example on a ReadTimeout, a ReadError or a RemoteProtocolError while the answer is being read. Path for an update: tools/drafts.py:save_update -> `context.erpnext.update(...)` raises the ErpnextError before `_wrote` runs. `meter.written` is still None, so tools/__init__.py:_attempt takes `if meter.written is None ...: return _refused(str(exc))`. The agent gets is_error with "ERPNext can't be reached (ReadError).", no comment goes on the draft, and no update description tells the agent the draft may have changed. Only the create descriptions say "After an error or a timeout, list the drafts". Path for the comment: tools/__init__.py:_comment catches the same ErpnextError from add_comment and returns "Enterich's comment couldn't be added to the draft: ERPNext didn't answer within 30 seconds.". When the operation's deadline runs out, the same function says more carefully that the comment "may be missing". Input: the PUT of an update reaches ERPNext, ERPNext saves it, and the connection drops, or the answer takes more than 30 s. The agent reports the update as not done, although ERPNext changed the draft.
proposal: Test (tests/unit/test_erpnext.py): give a fake transport that raises httpx2.ReadError for a PUT, call `Erpnext.update`, and assert that the error text says the change may have been saved and that the draft should be read before trying again. Also test a comment POST that times out and assert that the warning says the comment may be missing, not that it couldn't be added. Change: in `_call`, when `body is not None` or the method isn't GET, and the failure came after the request was sent (a timeout, or an HTTPError other than ConnectError/ConnectTimeout), raise a text such as "ERPNext didn't answer within 30 seconds; the change may have been saved: read the document before trying again.", or raise a separate ErpnextError subclass that callers can tell apart. In `_comment`, report that subclass with the same "may be missing" wording as the deadline case.

verdict.reason:
The code path is as the finding describes. src/enterich/erpnext.py:227-230 maps a TimeoutError or an httpx2.HTTPError to "ERPNext didn't answer within 30 seconds." or "ERPNext can't be reached (<Type>)." for every method, so a PUT that ERPNext saved but never answered reaches the agent as an error. But this doesn't meet the wrong-outcome bar, for four reasons.

(1) The text is true. It says ERPNext didn't answer or couldn't be reached. It never says nothing was written. Calling that implication "nothing was saved" is a complaint about wording, which is excluded.

(2) The specs chose how an unanswered write is handled. REQ-001-PRS-F015 (docs/specs/req-001-core.md:403) covers only "a create or update that ERPNext answered with the written draft". For an unanswered create, docs/specs/req-001-core.md:696 has the operation's description tell the agent to list the drafts after an error or a timeout; the create descriptions do this (e.g. src/enterich/tools/order_to_cash.py:433-434). Updates need no such note because of the `modified` lock (docs/specs/req-001-core.md:248, 255, 725), which the update descriptions state: "Give its `name` and its `modified` as last read; a draft changed since is refused" (src/enterich/tools/order_to_cash.py:450). If an update was saved without an answer and the agent retries, ERPNext refuses with TimestampMismatchError. The agent then re-reads the draft and sees the change. Nothing is lost and nothing is applied twice.

(3) For the comment: src/enterich/tools/__init__.py `_comment` puts a warning in the result holding ERPNext's own text ("didn't answer within 30 seconds"), and the draft is returned as written, as REQ-001-PRS-F015 requires ("If adding it fails or the time runs out, the result's warnings SHALL say so"). Whether that warning says "couldn't be added" or "may be missing" after a call timeout is wording, not a lost or false outcome.

(4) The proposed change would mean new spec behaviour for unanswered writes, not fixing code that breaks the current specs.

I ran nothing; reading the code was enough.

claim: A purchase return create can match two duplicate checks at once: a draft return against the same invoice, and the supplier's bill_no already recorded. The refusal names only the first match, so the agent decides on allow_duplicate without knowing about the bill_no match, and learns of it only in the warnings of a debit note that has already been written.
evidence: src/enterich/tools/returns.py:create builds `found = [Match(await same_invoice(...), RETURN_MATCH, "draft return")]`, appends `more` from `also` (procure_to_pay.create_draft_purchase_return's `same_bill`, `Match(names, BILL_MATCH, "purchase invoice")`), keeps `found = [m for m in found if m.names]`, then `if found and not allow_duplicate: raise drafts.refuse_duplicates(*found[0])`. Only `found[0]` reaches the refusal. With allow_duplicate true, `warnings = [drafts.duplicate_warning(*m) for m in found]` names both, but only after `drafts.insert`. Example: invoice PINV-1 of supplier S has a stale draft return DN-DRAFT made by the agent, and a submitted debit note DN-SUB of S already carries bill_no CN-77. A call to create_draft_purchase_return(return_against=PINV-1, bill_no=CN-77) is refused with "a draft return with the same invoice (return_against) exists (DN-DRAFT)". DN-SUB is not named. The agent knows DN-DRAFT is its own stale draft, so it repeats the call with allow_duplicate true. That inserts a second debit note for credit note CN-77, which is already booked, and the agent and the reviewer see DN-SUB named only in the new draft's warnings. REQ-001-PRS-F005 says the refusal SHALL name 'the matching documents', and REQ-005-PRS-F009 lists both matches for this create.
proposal: Test in tests/integration/test_return_drafts.py: seed a draft return against the purchase invoice and a submitted purchase invoice of the same supplier with bill_no CN-77. Call create_draft_purchase_return with bill_no CN-77 and without allow_duplicate. Assert that the refusal names both documents and that nothing was inserted. Change: in returns.create, build the refusal from every match in `found`, for example by joining one `refuse_duplicates`/`duplicate_warning`-style clause per Match into a single Refusal that names each kind and its documents, instead of passing `found[0]` alone.

verdict.reproduction:
Refusal path, src/enterich/tools/returns.py:230-235:
    found = [Match(await same_invoice(side, context, name), RETURN_MATCH, "draft return")]
    if also is not None and (more := await also(invoice)) is not None:
        found.append(more)
    found = [m for m in found if m.names]
    if found and not allow_duplicate:
        raise drafts.refuse_duplicates(*found[0])
Warning path, same function, src/enterich/tools/returns.py:237-238:
    warnings = [drafts.duplicate_warning(*m) for m in found]
    return await drafts.insert(context, side.invoice, doc, warnings), warnings
The second Match comes from src/enterich/tools/procure_to_pay.py:431-435 (`same_bill` -> `returns.Match(names, BILL_MATCH, "purchase invoice")`), passed as `also=same_bill` at procure_to_pay.py:444. drafts.refuse_duplicates (src/enterich/tools/drafts.py:123-127) takes one Match and names only its documents. Contract: REQ-001-PRS-F005 (docs/specs/req-001-core.md:261) says the refusal names "the matching documents", and REQ-005-PRS-F009 (docs/specs/req-005*.md:165) makes both the draft-return-against-the-invoice and the same-supplier bill_no matches for this create. So when both match, the refusal names only the draft return, and the bill_no match shows up only in the warnings after the insert. I did not run it. The code path is straight-line and reading it shows the result.
verdict.reason: I read returns.create (src/enterich/tools/returns.py:218-238), the `also` callback in procure_to_pay.create_draft_purchase_return (procure_to_pay.py:431-444), and drafts.refuse_duplicates and drafts.duplicate_warning (drafts.py:123-131). Nothing earlier stops both matches from being non-empty together: a draft return against PINV-1, plus a submitted or draft purchase invoice of the same supplier whose bill_no is CN-77. The refusal at line 235 takes found[0] only. The allow_duplicate path at line 237 names every match, so the two paths do not agree, and the refusal breaks REQ-001-PRS-F005's "naming the matching documents". A failing integration test fits: seed both matches, call without allow_duplicate, assert the refusal names both documents and nothing was inserted. The fix is a change to the code, within the current specs. claim: The fields every create or update result has are written twice: once as SAVED_FIELDS in tools/__init__.py, and again as a hand-typed tuple in the journal entry's result, which drops `status`. A field added to SAVED_FIELDS would reach every draft result except the journal entry's, and only for journal entries would the full result disagree with the fallback result _written builds from SAVED_FIELDS.
evidence: src/enterich/tools/__init__.py:50 `SAVED_FIELDS = ("name", "modified", "status", "docstatus", "company")` ("The fields of the saved draft every create or update result has"). drafts.result (drafts.py:341) uses `shape(saved, (*SAVED_FIELDS, *fields), ...)`, bank_and_cash._payment_result uses `(*SAVED_FIELDS, *PAYMENT_DRAFT_FIELDS)`, and _written uses `{k: saved[k] for k in SAVED_FIELDS if k in saved}`. But record_to_report.py:567 has `record = shape(saved, ("name", "modified", "docstatus", "company", *JOURNAL_DRAFT_FIELDS))`. REQ-001 Results say `status` appears "where its DocType has one", and REQ-006 says a journal entry has none. _written handles that with `if k in saved`; the journal result handles it by copying the list without `status`. Example: add `owner` to SAVED_FIELDS (and so to DRAFT_RESULT_FIELDS, which _write_text keeps when it slims a result). Every invoice, return and payment result then carries it, and so does a journal entry's _written fallback, but create_draft_journal_entry's normal result does not.
proposal: Test: for each create and update operation, the result holds every SAVED_FIELDS key the saved draft has. Patch SAVED_FIELDS in the test to add a field the fake journal entry returns, and the journal operations fail today. Change: build the journal record from SAVED_FIELDS itself, leaving out the fields its DocType lacks, e.g. `shape(saved, (*(f for f in SAVED_FIELDS if f != "status"), *JOURNAL_DRAFT_FIELDS))`. Better, give the tools module one helper, used by drafts.result, _payment_result, _journal_result and _written alike, that picks SAVED_FIELDS by whether the DocType has `status`.

verdict.reproduction: src/enterich/tools/__init__.py:49-50: `# The fields of the saved draft every create or update result has (REQ-001's Results)` / `SAVED_FIELDS = ("name", "modified", "status", "docstatus", "company")`. Used by drafts.py:341 `shape(saved, (*SAVED_FIELDS, *fields), outside=outside)`, bank_and_cash.py:480 `(*SAVED_FIELDS, *PAYMENT_DRAFT_FIELDS)`, and __init__.py:362 (_written's fallback) `**{k: saved[k] for k in SAVED_FIELDS if k in saved}`. Against that, src/enterich/tools/record_to_report.py:567 (_journal_result) `record = shape(saved, ("name", "modified", "docstatus", "company", *JOURNAL_DRAFT_FIELDS))` copies the list by hand without `status`. shapes.py:155 shape writes `doc.get(f)` for every field, so a missing `status` would come out as None; that is why the journal copy leaves it out, and why it can't simply reuse SAVED_FIELDS. If a maintainer adds a field to REQ-001's Results list (docs/specs/req-001-core.md:675) and so to SAVED_FIELDS, every invoice, return and payment result gets it, and so do DRAFT_RESULT_FIELDS (kept when _write_text slims a result) and a journal entry's _written fallback. create_draft_journal_entry and update_draft_journal_entry would not get it.
verdict.reason: Confirmed as one rule written twice. REQ-001's Results (docs/specs/req-001-core.md:675) set the fields every create or update result has, with `status` "where its DocType has one". REQ-006 (docs/specs/req-006-record-to-report.md:197) says a journal entry has no `status`. SAVED_FIELDS (src/enterich/tools/__init__.py:50) holds that list and three places build on it. _journal_result (record_to_report.py:567) types the same list again minus `status`, so adding a field to SAVED_FIELDS would not reach it. The difference is on purpose only for `status`, and nothing chose to keep the rest of the copy apart. Today both lists give the same output (journal entries have no status, and _written skips missing keys), so no test against the current SAVED_FIELDS fails. A test that patches SAVED_FIELDS would only be checking a made-up future change. So it is a proposal: a small restructure, e.g. build the journal record from SAVED_FIELDS minus `status`, or one shared helper that picks SAVED_FIELDS by whether the DocType has `status`. None of the listed patterns fits.

claim: The rule that a posting date sent to ERPNext goes with `set_posting_time` 1 is written out by hand in six places across order_to_cash.py and procure_to_pay.py, and drafts.due_dates depends on it. A change to what a fixed posting date sends, made in one place, would leave the others behind.
evidence: order_to_cash.py:259 `doc |= {"posting_date": inputs.posting_date.isoformat(), "set_posting_time": 1}`; order_to_cash.py:318 `fields: dict[str, Any] = {"posting_date": posting_date.isoformat(), "set_posting_time": 1}`; order_to_cash.py:338 the same; procure_to_pay.py:292 and procure_to_pay.py:415 the same; procure_to_pay.py:425-429 `"posting_date": posting_date.isoformat(), "set_posting_time": 1`. REQ-004 and REQ-005 each say Enterich SHALL send `set_posting_time` 1 whenever it sends a `posting_date`. drafts.due_dates (drafts.py:234) reads it back: `moves = not stored.get("set_posting_time") and stored.get("posting_date") != str(day)`. Example: a maintainer who makes the sales invoice's posting date also send its time, or who changes how a date is formatted, edits _invoice_body in one module. The sales returns and the purchase side keep the old pair. If one sender dropped `set_posting_time`, an update on a later day would move a date the agent fixed, and due_dates would rebuild the schedule from the wrong date.
proposal: Test: every invoice and return create or update given `posting_date` sends `set_posting_time` 1 next to it. Run it over all six operations as one parametrized test, so a new sender is covered too. Change: one helper in drafts, e.g. `def posted(day: date) -> dict[str, Any]: return {"posting_date": day.isoformat(), "set_posting_time": 1}`, used by both _invoice_body functions, _return_fields and the two return creates and updates.

verdict.reproduction:
One spec rule (REQ-004-OTC-F005, docs/specs/req-004-order-to-cash.md:106, and REQ-005, docs/specs/req-005-procure-to-pay.md:105: "SHALL send `set_posting_time` 1 whenever it sends a `posting_date`") is written out by hand in six places:

- src/enterich/tools/order_to_cash.py:318 (create_draft_sales_return) `fields: dict[str, Any] = {"posting_date": posting_date.isoformat(), "set_posting_time": 1}`
- src/enterich/tools/order_to_cash.py:338 (update_draft_sales_return) `fields |= {"posting_date": inputs.posting_date.isoformat(), "set_posting_time": 1}`

- src/enterich/tools/procure_to_pay.py:415 (_return_fields) the same

verdict.reason: I read all six senders in context: order_to_cash.py:250-345 and procure_to_pay.py:280-300 and 405-440. claim: The rule for a free-text reference that a duplicate check matches on (1–140 characters, no surrounding whitespace, not a name) is defined twice, as BillNo and as BankReference, with the same constraints and the same comment. A tightening made to one, such as refusing control characters as Name does, would leave the other's duplicate check open to the same evasion.
evidence: procure_to_pay.py:119-121: `# The supplier's invoice number as printed: free text, not a name (ERPNext's Data field); surrounding whitespace would defeat the duplicate check` and `BillNo = Annotated[str, Field(min_length=1, max_length=140, pattern=r"^\S(.*\S)?$")]`. bank_and_cash.py:132-134: `# The bank's reference for a payment, as on the statement: free text, not a name (ERPNext's Data field); surrounding whitespace would defeat the duplicate check` and `BankReference = Annotated[str, Field(min_length=1, max_length=140, pattern=r"^\S(.*\S)?$")]`. REQ-005 (`bill_no`) and REQ-007 (`reference_no`) state the same rule in the same words. The two types feed the same kind of check: _same_bill and _same_reference both match the value exactly with `=`. Example: something other than surrounding whitespace that ERPNext's exact match tells apart but a reviewer can't see, such as a zero-width character, gets refused in BillNo only. A payment's `reference_no` with the same character still passes the duplicate check.
proposal: Test: one parametrized test over `bill_no` (purchase invoice and return create and update) and `reference_no` (payment create and update) that feeds the same set of refused values, and expects each to be refused naming its input. Change: one type in shapes.py, e.g. `MatchedText = Annotated[str, Field(min_length=1, max_length=140, pattern=r"^\S(.*\S)?$")]` with the shared comment, and `BillNo = BankReference = MatchedText` (or the inputs using it directly).

verdict.reproduction: src/enterich/tools/procure_to_pay.py:119-121: `# The supplier's invoice number as printed: free text, not a name (ERPNext's Data field); # surrounding whitespace would defeat the duplicate check` / `BillNo = Annotated[str, Field(min_length=1, max_length=140, pattern=r"^\S(.*\S)?$")]` (used at :181, :192, :204, :213). src/enterich/tools/bank_and_cash.py:132-134: `# The bank's reference for a payment, as on the statement: free text, not a name (ERPNext's # Data field); surrounding whitespace would defeat the duplicate check` / `BankReference = Annotated[str, Field(min_length=1, max_length=140, pattern=r"^\S(.*\S)?$")]` (used at :220, :230). Specs: docs/specs/req-005-procure-to-pay.md:200 and docs/specs/req-007-bank-and-cash.md:182 both say "a string of 1–140 characters without leading or trailing whitespace, not a name". src/enterich/shapes.py:27-50 already hardens Name against control/format characters, the kind of tightening that would land in one of the two types and not the other. Nothing run: both behave the same today.
verdict.reason: Both types are the same constraint and give the same reason (ERPNext Data field length, surrounding whitespace would defeat an exact-match duplicate check). They feed the same kind of check, and nothing says they are meant to differ. So this is one rule written twice, not two values that happen to match. A maintainer hardening one duplicate check against invisible characters, as shapes.py:27-50 does for Name, would plausibly change only BillNo or only BankReference. No failing test shows it today because both behave the same, so the class is proposal and not fix. Merging them into one type in shapes.py is a restructure. Ideally it goes with a matching common-input line in REQ-001, since REQ-005:200 and REQ-007:182 each state the rule for their own input. None of the listed patterns fit.

claim: Which of an update's inputs are its changes (all fields except `name` and `modified`) is written twice. The update's at-least-one-change check uses one copy, and the draft comment's "given" list uses another, so a new identifying field added to DraftUpdate would still be counted as a given change in the comment unless both places are edited.
evidence: drafts.py:56 `changes = [field for field in type(self).model_fields if field not in ("name", "modified")]`. tools/__init__.py:121-123 in _origin: `named = [f for f in type(inputs).model_fields if f in given and f not in ("name", "modified")]`. REQ-001-PRS-F015 says the comment names "for an update, the inputs given besides `name` and `modified`", and every catalogue's update row says "**`name`**, **`modified`**; at least one of ...". Both copies spell out what those two fields are. Example: DraftUpdate gains a field that identifies the draft rather than changing it. _changes excludes it, so the update still needs a real change. _origin does not exclude it, so the ERPNext comment reads "given <that field>, ..." for an input that changed nothing, which misleads the person reviewing the draft.
proposal: Test: an update operation's comment names exactly the fields the inputs model counts as changes. Assert, for each update operation, that the names after "given" are a subset of the fields DraftUpdate._changes counts. Change: one constant on DraftUpdate, e.g. `KEYS = ("name", "modified")` or a classmethod `changes()` returning the change fields, used by both _changes and _origin.

verdict.reproduction: src/enterich/tools/drafts.py:56 (DraftUpdate._changes): `changes = [field for field in type(self).model_fields if field not in ("name", "modified")]` — the update's at-least-one-change check. src/enterich/tools/__init__.py:121-123 (_origin): `named = [f for f in type(inputs).model_fields if f in given and f not in ("name", "modified")]` — the comment's "given" list. Both write out the same rule, REQ-001-PRS-F015's "the inputs given besides `name` and `modified`", which is also the catalogues' "name, modified; at least one of ..." update rows. A grep finds no other copy and no shared constant. If a maintainer adds a field to DraftUpdate that identifies the draft, they will update the exclusion in _changes, which sits in the same class. _origin is in a different module and keeps its own tuple, so the comment would list that field after "given". The two copies agree today, so no test fails on the code as it is.
verdict.reason: I read both places in context. drafts.py:56 decides which DraftUpdate fields count as changes for the at-least-one check. tools/__init__.py:121-123 picks the given fields for the F015 comment, and it does so only for op.kind == "update", whose inputs are DraftUpdate subclasses. Both exclude the same two keys, and both stand for one rule in the spec (REQ-001-PRS-F015, docs/specs/req-001-core.md:403), so the match is not by chance and is not meant to differ. Neither the code nor an ADR gives a reason for the second copy. The bar is met: both places are quoted, and a plausible edit to one would leave the other behind. The class is proposal, not fix. Both copies behave the same today, so the change is a restructure: one source, such as a DraftUpdate constant or classmethod that _origin uses. ADR-008:49 says a restructure that no failing test shows is a proposal, made by hand in the code lens's first runs.

location: src/enterich/tools/returns.py:editable and src/enterich/tools/returns.py:not_a_return (called after drafts.editable in order_to_cash.update_draft_sales_invoice and procure_to_pay.update_draft_purchase_invoice)
claim: The payment and journal updates refuse a draft of the wrong kind through drafts.editable's `only`/`kind` check, which runs before the state, owner and `modified` checks. The invoice and return updates instead check return versus invoice by hand after drafts.editable has run all of those checks, so a wrong-kind draft that is also submitted, stale or another user's gets the state, stale or owner refusal instead of the operation that changes it.
evidence: src/enterich/tools/drafts.py:editable checks kind first: `if only and not any(all(stored.get(f) == v for f, v in m.items()) for m in only): raise Refusal(f"name: {name} isn't {kind}, ...")`, then `state = DOCSTATUS.get(...)`, the owner check and `if _timestamp(stored.get("modified")) != _timestamp(modified): raise Refusal(STALE)`. Its docstring says the kind is refused "before its state is told: the agent can read it, so it learns why it can't change it". bank_and_cash.update_draft_payment_entry and record_to_report.update_draft_journal_entry both pass `only=`/`kind=`. returns.editable does `stored = await drafts.editable(context, side.invoice, name, modified, side.what)` and only then `if not stored.get("is_return"): raise Refusal(f"name: {name} isn't a return; change it with {side.invoice_update}.")`. order_to_cash.update_draft_sales_invoice does `stored = await drafts.editable(context, "Sales Invoice", inputs.name, inputs.modified, "the sales invoice")` and then `returns.not_a_return(CREDIT_NOTES, stored)`; procure_to_pay.update_draft_purchase_invoice does the same. Input: update_draft_sales_invoice with the `name` of a draft credit note and an out-of-date `modified`. The answer is STALE ("get it again and repeat the update with its new `modified`"). The agent re-reads the draft and repeats the call, and only then hears "is a return; change it with update_draft_sales_return". The same call on a submitted credit note answers "is submitted; only drafts can be updated" and never names the return update. With the same inputs (stale or submitted), update_draft_payment_entry and update_draft_journal_entry name the kind first. tests/integration/test_record_to_report_drafts.py has a case "Stale as well: the refusal comes before the state and `modified` are checked". tests/integration/test_return_drafts.py:test_the_invoice_updates_refuse_a_return and test_the_return_updates_refuse_an_invoice use only current, unsubmitted drafts of the agent user.
proposal: Test: in tests/integration/test_return_drafts.py, parametrize test_the_invoice_updates_refuse_a_return and test_the_return_updates_refuse_an_invoice over a stale `modified` (and a submitted docstatus). Assert that the text starts with "name: ", names the other update operation, and that erp.writes() == []. This fails today with STALE or "is submitted". Change: run the return-versus-invoice check before drafts.editable's state, owner and `modified` checks. One option is to give drafts.editable a kind predicate with its own message (for example `refuse_kind: Callable[[dict], Refusal | None]`), called right after get_named where `only` is checked now. returns.editable would pass the "isn't a return" / "against no invoice" checks, and the invoice updates would pass returns.not_a_return. Then every update refuses a wrong-kind draft at the same point.

verdict.reason: The two places are meant to differ, so this isn't a missed pattern. drafts.editable's `only`/`kind` check (src/enterich/tools/drafts.py:184-188) is how the code meets REQ-001-PRS-F003 (docs/specs/req-001-core.md:232,242). That rule covers only "a kind its area spec rules out (another voucher type or payment type)", which no operation changes: the message ends "a person changes it in ERPNext". Only for those does the spec require the refusal "also when the draft is submitted or its `modified` is stale". REQ-001-bank-and-cash and REQ-006 cite that rule for payment and voucher types (docs/specs/req-007-bank-and-cash.md:92, docs/specs/req-006-record-to-report.md:106). A return and an invoice are not ruled out. Each is a kind the same area changes through its sibling operation. REQ-001-PRS-F025 (docs/specs/req-001-core.md:561,570) requires only that each update refuses the other's draft naming the operation that changes it, and it sets no order against the state, owner or `modified` checks. The order the code uses also makes sense. For a submitted credit note or another user's credit note, "change it with update_draft_sales_return" would mislead, because the return update refuses it too. The state or owner refusal (drafts.py:189-196) is the answer that helps. The code does not put every kind check first either: the journal update checks `multi_currency` after drafts.editable (src/enterich/tools/record_to_report.py:610), and the spec states that rule apart from the F003 kind. returns.editable (src/enterich/tools/returns.py:244-251) and returns.not_a_return (returns.py:255-259) after drafts.editable therefore follow the specs as written. Making them come first would change behaviour the specs leave open, not fix a bypassed helper.
